beats.text: Maya and her roommate Leo start YouTube channels on the same day.
Maya makes long videos. Ten minutes, cooking, one a week.
Leo only makes Shorts. Thirty seconds, every single day.
Same kitchen, same budget, same starting line.
Ninety days later, one of them has more views. The other has a stronger channel. And they're not the same person.
Let's follow both channels, and find out which format grows you faster, and why the real answer is: use both, the right way.
First, what makes a Short different?
A Short is a vertical video, up to three minutes long, watched in a feed you swipe through.
Nobody searches for it, and nobody picks it from a thumbnail. It just appears, and plays.
The viewer's only choice is: keep watching, or swipe away.
A long video works the other way around. The viewer sees a thumbnail and a title, decides to click, and commits minutes of their time.
Same platform. Two completely different ways of watching.
And that difference changes everything about how each one helps your channel.
So what makes a Short actually work?
It starts instantly. No intro, no greeting. The very first frame is already the interesting part.
It's about one thing only: one tip, one trick, or one result.
Text on screen helps, because lots of people scroll with the sound off.
And the best Shorts end in a way that makes people want to watch again, or see more.
In his first week, Leo's numbers explode.
One of his Shorts, a ten second egg trick, gets shown to thousands of people who have never heard of him.
That's the superpower of Shorts: discovery.
There's no click to earn. The feed puts your video in front of people for free, and lets them decide in a couple of seconds.
It's also low effort for the viewer. Watching thirty seconds is easy, so people try new creators all the time.
And Leo learns fast. Seven uploads a week means seven chances a week to see what works.
For a brand new channel, that kind of reach is hard to get any other way.
But by week four, Leo notices something strange.
His views are huge, but almost nobody comments. His subscribers don't watch his other videos.
A Short view can be a second of attention before the next swipe. People saw the egg trick. They didn't necessarily see Leo.
Many viewers subscribe to a feeling, not a person. They liked one clip, and they're gone.
And when Leo posts his first long video, his Shorts audience barely shows up.
Views are not the same as fans. Shorts are great at the first one, and slower at the second.
It's like meeting someone for two seconds at a party. They saw you. That doesn't mean they'll call.
Meanwhile, Maya's channel grows slowly. Her first month looks almost flat.
But look closer. Her viewers stay for minutes at a time. They comment, they ask questions, and they come back next week.
Long videos build trust. Ten minutes with someone's voice, face, and personality is how viewers become fans.
They're also findable. People search for things like cheap dinner ideas, and her videos can keep showing up for months, even years.
And one good long video leads to another. Viewers binge, and every hour they spend on her channel tells YouTube her videos are worth recommending.
Slower to start. But every view goes deeper.
A slow start isn't a bad start. It's just a different kind of growth.
What about earning money?
To join the YouTube Partner Program, a channel needs a thousand subscribers, plus one of two things.
Either four thousand watch hours from long videos in the past year.
Or ten million Shorts views in the past ninety days.
Both paths work. But once you're in, long videos usually earn more per view than Shorts.
So Shorts can help you get noticed, and long videos are usually where the steady income comes from.
Shorts ad money works differently too. It's pooled together, and shared between creators based on their share of views.
Let's check in on day thirty. These numbers are an illustration, not a promise.
Leo has hundreds of thousands of views, and about a thousand subscribers.
Maya has a few thousand views, and about two hundred subscribers.
Leo is ahead on reach. But compare how long people watch.
Maya's viewers have spent more total hours with her channel than Leo's have with his.
So who's winning? It depends on what you're counting.
So the roommates make a deal. They'll each steal the other's best move.
Maya starts cutting Shorts from her long videos. The sizzle, the reveal, the price tag.
Each Short is a trailer. It gives a taste, and points to the full video.
She uses the related video link on every Short, so one tap takes viewers to the long version.
Leo does the opposite. He takes his most popular Short, and turns it into a full ten minute deep dive.
And they keep the topics matched. A cooking Short leads to a cooking video, not a random vlog.
Shorts bring people in. Long videos give them a reason to stay.
Think of it like a restaurant. Shorts are the free samples outside. Long videos are the meal inside.
Here's the system Maya settles on.
One long video every week. That's the main course.
Then three Shorts cut from it: one on Monday, one on Wednesday, and one on Friday.
Each Short uses a different moment: a hook, a tip, and the final result.
She films everything on the same day, so the Shorts cost almost no extra time.
And every Sunday, she checks which Shorts sent people to the long video, and makes more like those.
That's four uploads a week, from a single filming day.
Along the way, both roommates make mistakes worth avoiding.
Leo's first mistake: Shorts on totally random topics. Each one found a different crowd, so none of them stuck around.
Maya's first mistake: uploading her Shorts sideways, with tiny text. On a phone, they were almost impossible to watch.
Another one: just chopping off the start of a long video. A Short has to make sense on its own, from the very first second.
And the biggest one: judging a Short in its first hour. Shorts can take days to find their audience, so give them time before you decide.
Day ninety. Again, the numbers are just an illustration.
Leo's Shorts still bring the biggest crowds, but now his long video gets real viewers too.
Maya's growth curve finally bends upward. Her Shorts bring new people, and her long videos keep them.
Both channels are growing faster than either one did alone.
Not because one format won. Because they stopped choosing.
And notice: neither of them quit when the numbers looked bad.
So, which should you make?
If you want to be discovered fast, and test ideas quickly, lean on Shorts.
If you want loyal viewers, search traffic, and steadier income, lean on long videos.
And if you want both, let your Shorts be the door, and your long videos be the room people want to stay in.
There's no wrong first step. The only real mistake is posting nothing while you decide.
Start this week: make one long video, and cut one Short from it.
